mcqs.question: An actor system has thousands of actors running concurrently. Within a single actor, can two messages ever be processed at the same time?
options: Yes, if the actor's mailbox has more than one pending message
Yes, but only for read-only messages
No, because actor systems only ever run one actor at a time system-wide
No — a single actor always processes its messages one at a time, sequentially, even though the system as a whole is deeply concurrent
mcqs.explanation: Concurrency in the actor model exists between actors, never within one — each actor processes its mailbox strictly sequentially, which is exactly what keeps its private state race-free without locks. Multiple actors do run concurrently system-wide, and message type (read vs write) doesn't change this per-actor sequential guarantee.

mcqs.question: A thousand `Increment` messages are sent concurrently to a single counter actor from a thousand different senders. Can the final count be wrong, the way the shared-memory counter from the previous topic was?
options: Yes, for the same read-modify-write reason as the threaded counter
Only if more than one actor instance exists
Yes, unless the actor explicitly acquires a lock before incrementing
No — the actor's mailbox serializes message handling, so each Increment is processed one at a time with no possibility of interleaving
mcqs.explanation: Because a single actor processes messages strictly one at a time, there's no way for two Increment operations to interleave the way two threads could — the race is structurally impossible, not merely locked against. No lock is needed (or used) inside the actor, and this holds regardless of how many senders exist.

mcqs.question: What's the key difference between "a mutex prevents a race" and "the actor model eliminates a race"?
options: There's no real difference — both approaches rely equally on developer discipline
A mutex only works if every code path remembers to acquire it; the actor model provides no syntax at all for one actor to directly touch another's state, making the bug structurally unrepresentable
Mutexes are always faster than actor-based isolation
The actor model still requires locks internally, just hidden from the developer
mcqs.explanation: A lock-based guarantee depends on consistent discipline across every access path; the actor model removes the capability to directly access another actor's state at all, so there's no path to forget to protect. Actors don't hide internal locks for this purpose, and the two approaches are not equivalent in reliability, regardless of relative performance.

mcqs.question: What is the core justification behind Erlang/Akka's 'let it crash' philosophy?
options: Crashing is always cheaper computationally than exception handling
Crashing avoids the need for any supervisor or restart logic at all
For most failures, restarting to a known-good state is more reliable than patching around the error in place with defensive code that might itself be wrong
It only applies to actors running on a single machine, not distributed ones
mcqs.explanation: The philosophy's actual claim is about reliability, not performance — resetting to clean state after most failures beats trying to defensively handle every possible error condition in place. It still requires a supervisor to actually perform the restart, and it applies identically to local and distributed actors thanks to location transparency.

mcqs.question: An actor system has been running fine for weeks and then suddenly runs out of memory with no obvious warning. What actor-specific failure mode should you suspect first?
options: An unbounded mailbox on a slow or stuck consumer actor silently accumulating messages faster than they're processed, until memory is exhausted
The supervisor tree restarted too many actors at once
Location transparency caused actors to duplicate themselves across machines
The actor model does not support memory allocation at all
mcqs.explanation: An unbounded mailbox accepting messages faster than a slow consumer can process them is a well-known, easy-to-miss actor failure mode that looks healthy from the outside right up until it isn't. Supervision restarts and location transparency don't inherently cause memory exhaustion, and actor systems obviously do allocate memory.

mcqs.question: Which bug class genuinely disappears entirely when moving from shared-memory threads to the actor model, rather than merely becoming less likely?
options: All logic bugs of every kind
Message-ordering assumptions that turn out to be wrong
Data races on shared mutable state, since no shared mutable state exists between actors
Mailbox backpressure issues
mcqs.explanation: Data races require shared mutable memory accessed concurrently; since actors never expose their state for direct external access, that specific bug class is structurally eliminated, not just reduced. Logic bugs, ordering assumptions, and mailbox backpressure are all failure modes that actors can still have.
